rv.q: Few writers of his generation have achieved anything quite like "The Humans," a play about the horrors of ordinary life and the love we need to counter them.

With or without those ominous suggestions that the American family as we know it is under existential threat, “The Humans” is a major discovery, a play as empathetic as it is clear-minded, as entertaining as it is honest.

The dark comedy opened Thursday at the Theatre with a terrific cast and an unsentimental look at the way we live today — anxiety-ridden, having little control over our environment or bodies, forever stretched and always a step from the abyss. It is an absolute triumph.
The only thing assured is the sound of laughter.
It is still the most, well, human play I've ever seen about fear and disappointment and the attachments that transcend them.
There is so much love, dread, tenderness and brutality in “The Humans” that it is hard to believe just 90 minutes pass through Stephen Karam’s deeply-felt family tragicomedy thriller.
That alone should keep this lovely play, an Off Broadway transfer, running in its inviting new Broadway house until kingdom come.
You’ll be glad you’ve been invited into the company of the Blakes, who themselves may fall short of glamorous but nevertheless help class up the whole darn neighborhood.

Even if the Blakes can't quite keep all the harsh realities of life at bay, Karam's empathetic rendering of a family enduring setbacks leaves the audience hopeful that they will find strength in their love for one another.

The Humans is just as funny, just as moving and just as sneakily unsettling in its new Broadway incarnation, and retains its essential intimacy.
I left the theater feeling that I'd just spent two whole hours there for no good reason.
Stephen Karam’s exquisite family drama, so lovingly transferred to Broadway, is a flawless gem.
The balance of suffering and solace in the play, which captures the way many middle-class Americans currently live better than anything else I've seen, is precise.
The finest new play of the Broadway season so far -- by a long shot.
If this is the best American family drama since August: Osage County, its method is quieter, sadder, and subtler than Tracy Letts' blackly humorous exercises in domestic combat.

This bestows upon what is, at least at first, a pretty typical dysfunctional-family drama new layers of depth, weight, and significance that make this as effective and affecting as anything the Main Stem has seen in years.
If you relish seeing a play that strikes out for unknown territories, that disturbs and provokes in equal measure then make a beeline to the play in question.
“The Humans” is monumentally affecting, and something for which theatergoers should be oh-so-very thankful.
Humans rather considers the trials its highly imperfect subjects face in a highly imperfect world, and resolves, without ever approaching sentimentality, that love is nonetheless resilient.
That's what's so beautiful and moving about "The Humans."
Thanks to Karam’s script and the ensemble’s performances, every slight, every shared memory, and every knowing glance feels utterly lived in.
Reflecting the times we're in, the problems we experience and the futures we can't control, the play isn't just a family portrait.
For all the problems the characters face, the actors are superb in communicating an affection and good humor that feels genuine and that draws us in.
Through brutal realism, Karam presents a family careering toward disaster with little in the way of an evasive action plan.
Karam effortlessly nails the brittle prickle of well-meant family reunions – of the generational friction of lives colliding over clung-to holiday traditions.
Nevertheless, it makes for a compelling and often terrifying character portrait.
Now that I've had a chance to revisit Karam's family drama at the Helen Hayes, I'm pleased to report that it does indeed offer a satisfying hour and a half in the theater.
When the curtain falls, you have no choice but to leave The Humans with a life altering worldview and for that, it is probably the best 90 minute therapy session money can buy.
It is impossible not to see yourself in The Humans, to see your mother, your father, and your siblings.
This play stuck with me for days after I saw it.
Under Joe Mantello's expert direction, the play walks a delicate line between a natural sort of comedy and a surreal, foreboding drama.
Steven Karam, best known for his 2011 drama Sons of the Prophet, establishes himself as one of America’s leading playwrights here with the saga of the Blakes.
One of the triumphs of Stephen Karam's stunning new work is how every one of the 90 or so minutes we spend with the Blakes seem blazingly authentic.

cn.t: Critics largely praise Karam's family drama as a deeply human, insightful work that captures middle-class anxiety with humor and compassion, elevated by Mantello's direction and superb ensemble performances.

sg.ra: Multiple guides converge on Rows B to H center as the best views in Broadway's smallest house (597 seats), where the intimate scale means these seats feel closer to the stage than premium orchestra in any other Broadway theater. The Hayes-specific tradeoff: patrons repeatedly flag that the stage sits unusually high for such an intimate room, so Row A and the very front can force neck-craning — one AVFMS viewer described the Hayes stage as 'particularly high for the first couple of rows, so you'll be using your neck to look up,' and a JOB patron noted 'The stage is high so you don't see actors' feet.' Rows B-H sit far enough back to clear that stage-height issue while still letting you read facial expressions in a house this small.

sg.vl: Value sweet spot where the rake kicks in
sg.ra: Rows F-M center are consistently flagged as the value band at Hayes — priced below premium but still close in a 597-seat room. The Hayes-specific reason to favor the back half of that band (J-M) over F-I: an AVFMS reviewer explicitly observed that 'Row J in the orchestra level is where the rake of the floor starts to increase so even a short guy like me can see over someone tall.' That makes J-M the first rows where a tall head in front stops being a problem, which matters more at Hayes than at larger houses because the orchestra is 'more long than it is wide' (NYTix) and the stage height is tall, so front-orchestra sightlines are flatter than usual.

The very back row of the Hayes mezzanine sits directly against the theater's staff/operations area — a quirk specific to this post-2018-renovation layout. Multiple AVFMS reviewers independently complain the ushers or crew are audible throughout the show from Mezz Row J: one wrote 'this row butts up against the row where the theater staff sits and they chatted, loudly, throughout the show'; another said 'the ushers downstairs were loud and I could sometimes hear their murmurings'; an accessible-seat user at Mezz J-101 reported 'there's some sort of operation booth to the right of this seat and it's very loud and distracting. I could hear talking and typing throughout the entire show.' Because Hayes is the smallest house on Broadway, there's no orchestra noise to mask ambient staff chatter the way a 1,500-seat venue would — in this intimate room, the booth chatter carries.
